rewrite.hint: The rule has to tell a keyword from the same letters inside a string. That needs the code's grammar, not its characters.
rewrite.explanation: A parser turns source text into an abstract syntax tree, where the loop is a node and the await expression inside it is a child node; strings and comments have already become their own node types, so they cannot be mistaken for code. A regular expression sees only characters, which is why text search matches the word inside a comment. Minified output and stack traces come later and no longer carry the original structure, so neither can answer a question about the source.

rationale: Destination: general L7 'How Code Runs', which already teaches compiler, interpreter, JIT, transpilation and bundling but never says what those tools operate on, and no active item anywhere in the bank mentions a syntax tree. Reformulated around a lint rule, the objective explains why structural tools succeed where find-and-replace over text corrupts code.
evidence: knowledge: parsers produce an abstract syntax tree; linters and codemods match against its node types rather than against source characters

rewrite.question: A multiplayer game sends player positions many times a second. When one update is lost, resending it is worse than skipping it, because a newer position has already gone out. Which transport fits this traffic?
options: UDP, because it sends datagrams best-effort and never resends a lost one
TCP, because it retransmits lost segments until every byte arrives
TCP, because its ordering guarantee keeps the positions consistent
HTTP, because it already runs over a reliable connection
rewrite.hint: A resent update would arrive after a newer one. Ask which transport is willing to let the lost packet go.
rewrite.explanation: UDP sends independent datagrams with no retransmission and no ordering, so a lost position update is simply replaced by the next one to arrive. TCP would hold later data back while it resends the missing segment, which adds delay to updates that are already stale; its ordering guarantee imposes the same cost. Reliability is the right default for a file transfer or an API call, and the wrong trade for data that expires in milliseconds.

rationale: Destination: general L2 'Clients & Servers', which teaches clients, servers, reverse proxies and load balancers and mentions the TCP connection in rm-general-12 without ever saying what reliability costs; no active item in the bank mentions UDP. Reformulated with reasoning-bearing options, it teaches the latency-versus-reliability trade that also explains why HTTP/3 moved onto QUIC.
evidence: knowledge: UDP delivers independent datagrams with no retransmission or ordering guarantee, while TCP's in-order delivery causes head-of-line blocking
